dialogs.title: Діалог — Monday morning, three months after Unit 1
dialogs.intro: The last conversation in this book uses almost everything you've learned: past, future, seven cases, and the calling form. Read it once without looking at the translation. If you can follow it, you're A1.

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: Wonderful! On Saturday I went to St. Sophia's Cathedral.
lines.literal: wonderful! on — Saturday (accusative) — I — was (past f) — in — Sophia's (locative) — cathedral.

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: Very much. And on Sunday Andriy and I went for a walk in Podil.
lines.literal: very. and — on — Sunday — we — with — Andriy (instrumental) — walked — in — Podil.

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: A little. But we had coffee in a small coffee shop.
lines.literal: a-little. but — we — drank (past pl) — coffee (accusative) — in — small (locative) — coffee-shop.

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: And what are you two doing next week?
lines.literal: and — what — you — will-do — next (genitive) — week?

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: I don't know yet. Maybe we'll go to Lviv.
lines.literal: not — know. maybe, will-ride — to — Lviv (genitive).

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: Good idea. Lviv is very beautiful.

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: Oksana, can I ask a question?

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: Ani, you just talked with me for ten minutes. In Ukrainian.
lines.literal: Ani, you — just — talked (past f) — with — me (instrumental) — ten — minutes. in-Ukrainian.

notes: **Days take у + знахідний (accusative).** *У понеділок*, *у середу*, *у п'ятницю*, *у суботу*, *у неділю*. Notice that feminine days change their ending (*середа* → *середу*), while masculine ones don't (*понеділок* stays *понеділок*).

**Ми з Андрієм means "Andriy and I", not "we with Andriy".** This pattern is typical of Slavic languages and feels odd at first: Ukrainian uses *ми* (we) for two people, one of whom is the speaker. *Ми з мамою* = Mom and I. *Ми з тобою* = you and I.

**Сподобалося is neuter because the thing liked isn't named.** If it is named, the ending follows it: *Мені сподобався собор* (m), *Мені сподобалася кав'ярня* (f). Back to Unit 15: the flipped sentence.

**Робитимете is the one-word future.** Oksana could just as well say *будете робити*, and it would mean exactly the same. This one-word form is the one Russian doesn't have, and using it now and then is a mark of real Ukrainian.
**Може means "maybe", not "he can".** Two words spelled the same: *може* (maybe, an adverb) and *може* (he/she can, from *могти*). Context tells them apart. A clearer alternative: **можливо**.

**Оксано: the calling form, once more.** Ani now uses it naturally, which she didn't do in Unit 1. This is the seventh case, the one Russian doesn't have, and to Ukrainians it sounds like a sign that you're really learning their language.
**Щойно = just now.** For something that has just finished, seconds or minutes ago. Its relatives: *тільки що* (just), *недавно* (not long ago), *давно* (long ago).

grammars.title: Days of the week
after: The day names tell a story: **понеділок** means "after неділя", **вівторок** comes from "second", **середа** from "middle", **четвер** from "fourth", **п'ятниця** from "fifth". Only *субота* (from Sabbath) and *неділя* ("not doing") come from outside the count.

grammars.title: Seven cases, one word
body: Here is the whole book summed up in one table. The word *сестра* (sister) goes through all seven of its cases, and every row is a unit you've already worked through.
after: If this table makes sense to you now (not memorized, but recognized from the sentences), then this book has done its job.

blocks.title: What you can do now
items: **Greet people, introduce yourself, and address people correctly**, including the кличний (vocative) form that Russian doesn't have.
**Talk about yourself**: where you're from, family, job, where you live, age, hobbies.
**Get through everyday life**: order food, shop, ask prices and directions, buy medicine.
**Move through three tenses**: tell about yesterday, describe today, plan tomorrow, with two different ways to form the future.
**Use all seven cases in the singular**: not perfectly, but well enough to be understood in every sentence you say.
About **three hundred words**, enough for eight out of ten everyday conversations a newcomer has.
**Plurals in every case.** So far you've almost always dealt with one thing. Plurals add one more layer, but you already know the patterns.

**Verb aspect**: pairs like *читати / прочитати*, *писати / написати*. The difference between "doing" and "done", which English shows only partly (*was reading* vs. *read it through*), and which decides more than anything whether your Ukrainian sounds natural.
**Adjectives in the other cases.** So far you've used adjectives only in their basic form; at A2 they change along with their noun.
**Subordinate clauses.** *Я знаю, що…*, *Я думаю, що…*, *Якщо…, то…*: the door to telling stories, not just answering questions.

blocks.text: One last piece of advice, and it isn't grammar: **start speaking before you feel ready.** The bar for "good enough" is much lower than beginners imagine, and Ukrainians are among the warmest people toward foreigners who try their language. Case mistakes don't stop people from understanding you; staying silent for fear of mistakes does.
